title: Exhortations to Excellence
author: Patrick Whalen
summary: Patrick Whalen's essay opens with a vivid scene from his 2007 Marine Corps School of Infantry training: a 20km forced march with over 100 pounds of gear, body armor chafing skin. In this context, a Gunnery Sergeant delivered an exhortation combining classical citations with direct challenge before the march began. The essay argues that real excellence is neither comfortable nor self-congratulatory -- it requires being pushed by someone who believes you are capable of more than you currently think. Whalen draws on the Pindar tradition of fire as the metaphor for excellence, reflecting on how the capacity to be genuinely exhorted depends on being in a context where someone actually demands it. The piece is both personal and philosophical: a defense of challenge, discomfort, and the relational context that makes excellence possible rather than merely aspired to.
points: * Genuine excellence requires being exhorted -- pushed past the ceiling of what you currently think you can do -- by someone who demands more than praise. * Environments that expect excellence and apply real consequences for failure produce a different kind of person; comfort produces a different kind of person. * Exhortation is a relational act, not just a motivational speech: it requires someone who actually believes in your capacity and challenges you on that belief. * The capacity to receive exhortation -- to be moved by someone's demand rather than resentful of it -- is itself a cultivated virtue that distinguishes exceptional performers. * The Pindar fire metaphor connects the moment to a long tradition: excellence is kindled by others, not just discovered within oneself.
quotes: In 2007 I was finishing up the Marine Corps' School of Infantry, my last stop before joining an infantry unit in the operational forces, or "the fleet" as we called it.
I was the "guide" for my platoon which meant that I was the trainee responsible for overseeing some of the more mundane duties necessary for the functioning of a training platoon.
That particular morning we were hustling out of the training barracks and onto the "grinder" where we staged our gear in preparation for a 20km hump through the mountains of Camp Pendleton.
Most of us were carrying over 100lbs including our packs, body armor, and weapon systems, but depending on the specific job (rifleman, machine-gunner, mortar-man) some were carrying much more.
Early mornings in Southern California's coastal mountains are beautiful and fragrant with chapparal, and we saw many--probably all of them--during our time in training to become infantrymen.
But that morning, overpowering the fresh salt and chapparal in the air was a sense of dread and fear.
We all knew that the next several hours would be physically miserable.
